ext.research_question: How can social network analysis of a single US dark money network (politically active nonprofits that take unlimited donations without disclosing donors) be made more rigorous by (a) ranking key nodes with a multi-criteria method (AHP/TOPSIS) instead of a subjective choice of centrality measure, and (b) turning the State-versus-network contest into a game with cardinal payoffs so that kinetic (prosecution/legislation) versus non-kinetic (exposure via press) strategy mixes can be solved for (Sections 1-2, 4; abstract).
ext.data: No new sample. The unit is the organization (node) in one dark money network (DMN) that the authors analyzed in earlier unpublished work. Network-level description: a money-flow network in which ties mean funds were exchanged, node size is betweenness, tie width is dollar amount, and some nodes attended a strategy event (Figure 1, Section 1). Analytic set: the 8 organizations with the highest overall degree centrality, computed in ORA (Table 1, Section 2). Centrality values come from ORA, which lists only the top ten per metric, so some organizations have missing values (Section 4). Expert inputs: AHP pairwise judgments by the authors on Saaty's nine-point scale (criteria weights, Table 4, CR = 0.062; game payoffs, CR = 0.02244 for State and 0.03248 for DMN). No time period is stated for the network data. The number of nodes in the full DMN and the dollar amounts are not reported numerically.
ext.method: Three linked components. (1) AHP criterion weighting over eight SNA measures (out-degree, total degree, eigenvector, betweenness, hub, in-degree, closeness, authority), with out-degree ranked first (weight 0.50199) and authority last (0.03418) (Table 2, Table 4, Section 2). (2) TOPSIS ranking of the 8 organizations on the unscaled ORA values using those weights (Table 5). Sensitivity analysis follows Alinezhad and Amini (Eq. 1): change one weight in 0.1 steps and rescale the others proportionally (Section 3). (3) Game theory on a 2x2 State (non-kinetic A vs kinetic B) by DMN (maintain centralized C vs decentralize D) game. Ordinal ranks 1-4 (Table 6) are converted to cardinal utilities by AHP (Table 7). Solutions use Nash equilibrium, mixed equalizing strategies, prudential (security-level) strategies and Nash arbitration (Feix solver; Fox lottery-alternative approach). A 5-action State vs 2-action DMN extension uses 10 strategies and a nonlinear program (Barron, Equation 2), solved in Maple 15 (Section 4).
ext.identification: None. This is a descriptive decision-analysis and modeling paper with no causal identification strategy, no treatment or comparison group, and no estimation of effects from data. Robustness is checked only by one-weight sensitivity analysis (Section 3).
ext.scope: Population: one US politically active dark money network of nonprofits and linked LLCs (SMLLCs), with the State modeled as the opposing player. Institutional frame: IRS rules on 501(c) political activity and disclosure, with sources cited to 2010-2014 news and IRS materials (accessed 2014-2015). The paper says the network is currently legal and that the State's kinetic options are prosecution, fines and legislation. Methodological scope is general: the authors state the method applies to any dark network. Era: circa 2010-2015 (inferred from cited sources and access dates).

key_findings.finding: Out-degree is weighted most heavily (0.50199), followed by total degree (0.14517) and eigenvector (0.11045); the AHP consistency ratio is 0.062, under the 0.10 threshold.

TOPSIS ranks Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce first, Center to Protect Patients' Rights second, and Corner Table LLC third. Corner Table has low out-degree (7) but ranks third. TC4 Trust, third in out-degree (38), ranks seventh. Only the top two organizations match the out-degree ranking.
key_findings.numbers: TOPSIS closeness: 0.7538 (FPCC, out-degree 90), 0.6192 (CPPR, out-degree 78), 0.4909 (Corner Table, out-degree 7), 0.4887 (American Future Fund), 0.4869, 0.4837, 0.4835 (TC4 Trust, out-degree 38), 0.4817

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity: raising out-degree weight in 0.1 steps until it is no longer the largest weight leaves Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce ranked first. Raising the lowest weight (closeness) lets Center to Protect Patients' Rights overtake Freedom Partners.
key_findings.numbers: Figures only; no numeric thresholds given in text

key_findings.finding: Ordinal game equilibrium is AD (State non-kinetic, DMN decentralize). Cardinal AHP utilities give State values AD 0.480038, BD 0.28523, AC 0.139265, BC 0.095467 (CR 0.02244) and DMN values BC 0.480645, BD 0.290615, AD 0.137848, AC 0.090892 (CR 0.03248).
key_findings.numbers: State and DMN AHP utilities as listed; Nash equilibrium AD at (0.48, 0.137)

key_findings.finding: Mixed equalizing strategy for the State is non-kinetic 84.8385% and kinetic 15.1615%. The paper says this replaces the earlier 50/50 recommendation, and the authors conclude that about 85% of effort should go to non-kinetic methods.
key_findings.location: Section 4 and Section 5, p. 349-351 and p. 352

key_findings.finding: Prudential (security-level) strategies: State plays A (non-kinetic) and DMN plays C (centralize) always, with security levels 0.139 for the State and 0.137 for the DMN.
Nash arbitration places the outcome near BD, projected to the Pareto segment at about (0.31, 0.3192).

Ten-strategy extension (decomposed actions A1-A3 kinetic, B1-B2 non-kinetic) with a nonlinear program. Solution: State randomizes between two actions with weights 0.92 and 0.8 (as printed), and DMN centralizes with probability 1. The objective value is Z = -0.001129 at p = 0.084, q = 0.0595.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Equation 2 and the solution after it, p. 351-352

limitations: The authors say explicitly that no significant changes resulted from the MADM analysis, though the findings were improved (Section 5, p. 352).

All criterion weights and game payoffs come from the authors' own subjective pairwise judgments on Saaty's scale. No external validation of weights or payoffs is reported. Sensitivity checks cover only one weight changed at a time (Section 3).

Single network, eight alternatives, unknown time period, and no reported N for the full network. Findings cannot be generalized to other dark networks without further study, although the authors state the method applies to any dark network.
ORA reports only the top ten nodes per metric, so some centrality values are missing for lower-ranked organizations (Section 4).

Kinetic and non-kinetic are defined by the authors: kinetic means IRS-related prosecution or fines, legislation on non-profit political activity, donation transparency and LLC anonymity rules; non-kinetic means press exposure of donors (Section 4, p. 348). The payoff structure depends on these definitions.

Game results depend on the assumed payoff framing. The authors state that anonymity and money flow are the DMN's main goals. The paper also includes a partisan framing of the opposing side ('Liberal leadership in the United States is unable to conduct' kinetic operations, Section 4), which is the authors' premise, not a tested finding.

The 10-strategy nonlinear solution as printed is internally inconsistent. The reported x2 = 0.92 and x4 = 0.8 sum to 1.72, not 1 as the constraint requires, and the text describes 92% and 8% shares. The likely intended value is 0.08, but this is not confirmed in the paper, so the reported solution is unverified.
Game-theory analysis treats the State and the DMN as two rational players with fixed payoffs. Structural dynamics such as DMN adaptation or donor response are not modeled.
Sources are news and advocacy reports from 2010-2014 (for example references 13, 15, 16, 18, 19), and the authors do not state dollar amounts or donor counts for the network analyzed.
measures: ORA social network centrality: out-degree, in-degree, total degree, eigenvector, closeness, betweenness, hub and authority centrality
AHP criterion weights (Saaty nine-point scale) and consistency ratio (CR)
TOPSIS closeness coefficient (larger is better) for ranking 8 organizations
Sensitivity of rank to one weight changed in 0.1 steps with proportional rescaling (Equation 1)
Ordinal payoffs 1-4 converted to cardinal AHP utilities; Nash equilibrium, prudential security levels, mixed equalizing strategy, Nash arbitration value, nonlinear program objective Z
ext.theory: Dark network analysis from the social network analysis literature (covert networks, key-node identification by centrality), combined with multi-criteria decision analysis (AHP and TOPSIS) and two-player game theory with cardinal utility (Nash equilibrium, Nash arbitration, security levels). The paper cites Krebs (2002) and Everton (2012) and argues for disrupting donor anonymity through targeted removal of nodes or through press exposure.

rel.summary_md:
Couch, Fox and Everton (2016) take one US dark money network: politically active nonprofits and linked single-member LLCs that pass money between them without disclosing donors. They apply two decision-analysis tools to it. First, they rank the 8 organizations with the highest degree using TOPSIS over eight ORA centrality measures. The authors set the weights themselves through AHP pairwise judgments. Out-degree gets 0.502, total degree 0.145, eigenvector 0.110 and betweenness 0.075, with a consistency ratio of 0.062. Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce ranks first (closeness coefficient 0.754), and the ranking survives a one-weight-at-a-time sensitivity sweep. Only the top two match the plain out-degree order, and the authors admit the method produced "no significant changes". Second, they model State versus network as a 2x2 game with payoffs from AHP. The State's equalizing mix is about 85% exposure through the press and 15% prosecution or legislation. There is no outcome data, no time window and no validation, and the 10-strategy solution as printed is inconsistent (0.92 + 0.8 is not 1).

For Paul's systems the paper is mainly a caution about scope and method, not evidence. Mentat's PAC transfer graph follows only FEC-reported committee cash, so it cannot see the nonprofit layer this paper maps. The retired cosponsor InfluenceScore has the same shape as the paper's composite: a hand-weighted mix of centralities led by out-degree. Neither the paper nor the system checks such a composite against an outcome. The paper's AHP consistency ratio and one-weight sensitivity sweep are reusable ways to document owner-judgment weights such as the pillar blend. They do not make those weights valid. The game theory section has no counterpart in the system.

bearings.paper_claim: The dark money network is a money-flow graph among 501(c) nonprofits and SMLLCs. Ties mean funds exchanged and tie width is the dollar amount. Its defining feature is unlimited donations with no donor disclosure. The authors map it from news and IRS sources from 2010-2014, not from FEC filings. The top node, Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce, has out-degree 90.
bearings.paper_location: Section 1 and Figure 1, p. 343-345; Table 1 and Table 5, p. 346-347
bearings.system_side: Mentat walks FEC-reported committee-to-committee edges breadth-first to depth 3. allocate() spreads each root's funding pro rata over observed outflows, conserves cents, and puts unattributable dollars in unresolved buckets (depth_limit, cycle, no_observed_outflow). Opposition stays with the named target. The docstring says the result is a conditional pro-rata scenario, not traced dollars. Nothing upstream of a reporting committee enters the graph.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This carries over only as a scoping statement. Industry money that passes through a non-disclosing nonprofit before reaching a super PAC appears in FEC data, at most, as one contributor row naming the nonprofit, so its sources are invisible to Mentat. The paper gives no data source or method for that hidden layer: its edges come from journalism. The network is from about 2010-2015 and is a single partisan donor network. Do not import its centrality ranking as evidence about any industry Mentat tracks. Any key-node ranking on Mentat's committee graph would be a heuristic output (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: The paper builds a composite from expert-weighted centralities: out-degree 0.50199 first, then total degree 0.14517, eigenvector 0.11045 and betweenness 0.07489 (CR 0.062). TOPSIS on this composite agrees with the plain out-degree order only for the top 2 of 8. Corner Table LLC has out-degree 7 and ranks 3rd; TC4 Trust has out-degree 38 and ranks 7th. The authors concede that no significant changes resulted, and they validate the ranking against no outcome.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2, Tables 2, 4 and 5, p. 346-347; Section 5, p. 352
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore = 0.60 x max-normalized weighted out-degree + 0.25 x betweenness + 0.15 x eigenvector, rescaled to 0-100. The weights are hand-set. The score was retired from the Influence pillar (AB13 = 0) as direction-blind but still feeds the underdog lens.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The two composites are built the same way: judgment weights led by out-degree. The paper adds a consistency check and a sensitivity sweep, but it does not show that the composite tracks any criterion. It cannot justify the 0.60/0.25/0.15 weights or reverse the retirement. Its ties are dollar flows among nonprofits, not cosponsorship. Sotoudeh et al. 2024 remains the relevant test: does centrality predict bill passage?

bearings.paper_claim: The paper elicits criterion weights by AHP pairwise comparison on Saaty's 9-point scale and accepts them only if the consistency ratio is under 0.10 (here 0.062). Its robustness test, following Alinezhad and Amini (Eq. 1), changes one weight in 0.1 steps, rescales the others proportionally and tracks rank changes. Under that sweep the top-ranked node holds, while raising the lowest weight lets the second-ranked node overtake the first.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2, Table 3-4, p. 346-347; Section 3, Equation 1 and Figures 4-5, p. 347
bearings.system_side: The pillar weights are owner policy, not estimated: Leg 0.45 / Press 0.10 / Influence 0.40 / Demo 0.05 live, unratified (S-5 open). The record conflicts on whether the ratified set was 30/25/40/5 or 25/30/40/5. One open question is how sensitive top-133 membership is to the weight set.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The one-at-a-time proportional rescaling sweep can be used directly to answer the open top-133 sensitivity question. AHP would only document the owner's judgment and check that it is internally consistent. It produces no outcome validity, and the paper's own weights are unvalidated. Treat any AHP-derived weight set as owner policy with a CR label, never as an estimate.

gaps_exposed: Mentat has no non-disclosing nonprofit (501(c)(4)/(c)(6), SMLLC) layer upstream of reporting committees. Industry money routed through such conduits enters the transfer graph only at the receiving committee, so attributed industry totals are a lower bound on that channel. The paper shows this layer exists and is organized as a network.

No recorded weight-sensitivity sweep exists for the four-pillar blend. A one-weight-at-a-time proportional-rescale sweep (paper Eq. 1) is a cheap answer to the open question on top-133 overlap between weight sets.

Owner-judgment tables (pillar weights, IMP weights, SGATE, PERS) have no documented elicitation or internal-consistency check. AHP's consistency ratio is one way to record that judgments are at least coherent. It would not validate them.
Neither the paper nor the system validates a weighted-centrality composite against an outcome. The retired InfluenceScore still feeds the underdog lens without such a test.
flags: D-025: the paper calls TOPSIS output a 'closeness coefficient' and frames high scorers as key or influential nodes. If any of this is ported, label it a heuristic model output: not network closeness, access, or influence probability.
The paper's weights and game payoffs are the authors' own Saaty-scale judgments with no external validation. Do not cite it as evidence that out-degree should dominate a centrality composite.
The 10-strategy nonlinear-program solution as printed is internally inconsistent: x2 = 0.92 and x4 = 0.8 sum to 1.72. Do not quote it.
The game's premise contains a partisan framing of the State player, which is the authors' assumption, not a finding. Keep it out of any Melange or Mentat surface.

Coincidence only: the legacy workbook's Primary Layer weight row also contains 0.80 (likely meant to be 0.08) and also sums to 1.72 (brain actors/moneyball-workbook-lineage-and-june-audit.md:61). The June presentation audit recorded that independently. There is no relation to this paper.

This analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization) is argued for here. Tie width = dollars is display, not normalization.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper. The component list cites it only as 'on disk' under the PAC transfer graph, next to his note linking dark-money giving to Furnas's ideological infrastructure. The paper supports the idea that a dark-money organization network is real and can be mapped. It also shows that this network sits upstream of anything Mentat's FEC-only graph can trace, which his notes do not address. On centrality, Paul says more research on forms of centrality is needed. The paper's answer is to weight several centralities by expert judgment (AHP/TOPSIS), but it never validates the result. It therefore does not resolve his question and does not reverse the system's retirement of direction-blind centrality. His Sotoudeh highlight (eigenvector is 'not a strong indicator of bill passage') remains the more relevant evidence.

related.why: Irvin investigates how dark money operates across US nonprofit advocacy organizations. That is the population this paper samples one network from, and it can give the scope and prevalence this single-network study lacks.
Sotoudeh tests whether cosponsorship centrality predicts bill passage. That outcome validation is exactly what the AHP/TOPSIS composite here never does.
Both papers face the same choice of which centrality to use. Ardekani picks Katz on substantive grounds, while this paper weights eight centralities by expert judgment.
Gaynor builds directed money-flow networks among political organizations (leadership PACs to caucus members), the same kind of financial-tie object this paper analyzes for nonprofits.
Ringe et al. treat network centrality as a measure of political influence. Their work is a contrast case for whether a centrality ranking stands for real power, which this paper simply assumes.
